english: to be few; to be little (in amount)
usage: to be not few (= quite a lot)
litotes; a polite way to say 'a fair amount'
examples: 사람이 적어요.
There are few people.
subject takes 이/가, and the verb stays an adjective: 적어요, never 적어 있어요
요즘 일이 적어서 한가해요.
I have little work these days, so I'm free.
적어서 (-아서) links the small amount to its result, being free
월급은 적지만 일이 재미있어서 다녀요.
The pay is low, but the work is fun, so I keep going.
real-life register: 적다 is the normal word for low pay/salary, paired here with the concessive -지만
nuance: 적다 means small in QUANTITY — few in number or little in amount — and never small in physical SIZE. The killer pitfall for English speakers is that 'small' covers both, so they reach for 작다 (small size) when they mean 적다 (small amount); the two even sound close. Rule of thumb: if you could put a number on it (사람, 돈, 시간, 양), use 적다; if you could measure it with a ruler (가방, 방, 손), use 작다. Its opposite is 많다 (many/much), not 크다. Don't confuse the adjective 적다 with the adverb 조금/적게 either: 'There's little money' is 돈이 적어요 (adjective describing the money), while 'eat a little' is 조금/적게 먹어요 (adverb describing how you eat). A natural near-synonym is 모자라다 (to fall short/be insufficient), but 모자라다 implies 'not enough for the need,' whereas 적다 is just a neutral 'small amount.'

Using 적다 as if it were a verb: 돈이 적어 있어요 is wrong. 적다 is a descriptive adjective, so it's simply 돈이 적어요.
Confusing the adjective with the adverb: for 'eat less' don't say 적어 먹어요; the adverb form is 적게 먹어요 or 조금 먹어요.

usage: to be slow on one's feet
adverb 느리게 describes the action's pace
to be slow to act / sluggish
examples: 인터넷이 느려요.
The internet is slow.
everyday complaint; 느리다 → 느려요 in the 해요-form
이 버스는 너무 느려서 답답해요.
This bus is so slow it's frustrating.
느려서 (-아서) ties the slowness to the feeling it causes
죄송하지만 조금 느리게 말씀해 주시겠어요?
Sorry, but could you speak a little more slowly?
real-situation polite request using the adverb 느리게 + honorific 말씀하다
nuance: 느리다 describes LOW SPEED — a slow bus, slow internet, a slow walker — and its opposite is 빠르다 (fast). The single biggest trap for English speakers is mixing it up with 늦다, because English 'slow' and 'late' both feel like 'not fast'; but 느리다 is about RATE OF MOTION while 늦다 is about being LATE IN TIME relative to a deadline. The internet being 느리다 (slow) has nothing to do with you being 늦다 (late) for the meeting. There is a second near-synonym worth knowing: 이르다 means 'early (in time),' the time-opposite of 늦다, so the two pairs are 느리다↔빠르다 (speed) and 이르다↔늦다 (timing) — keep the axes separate. 느리다 collocates with 속도 (speed), 발 (feet, = slow-footed), and 행동 (movement/action). It is a plain, neutral word usable in any register, and as an adjective it cannot take 있다: say 버스가 느려요, never 버스가 느려 있어요.

mistakes: Using 느리다 to mean 'I'm late': 회사에 느렸어요 is wrong. Being late for something is 늦다 → 회사에 늦었어요.
Swapping the time-word and speed-word: 'the train is early' is 기차가 일러요 (이르다), not 기차가 느려요 — 느리다 only covers slow speed.
Treating 느리다 like a verb: 차가 느려 있어요 is incorrect; it's a descriptive adjective, so 차가 느려요.

usage: 낮다 covers low numbers/levels, not just height
낮다 also means low in pitch
낮다 + -아지다 = a change to a lower state
examples: 이 의자는 낮아요.
This chair is low.
낮다 → 낮아요; describes height off the ground
오늘은 기온이 낮아서 패딩을 입었어요.
The temperature is low today, so I wore a padded coat.
낮아서 (-아서) links the low temperature to the resulting action
요즘 금리가 낮아서 대출받기 좋아요.
Interest rates are low these days, so it's a good time to take out a loan.
real-situation: 낮다 is the natural word for low rates/levels in news and finance talk
nuance: 낮다 means LOW on a scale — low in height off the ground, low temperature, low price, low level, or low pitch — and its opposite throughout is 높다 (high). The classic English-speaker pitfall is using 낮다 for a SHORT PERSON, because English says 'low/short' loosely; but a person's shortness is 키가 작다 (small in stature), never 키가 낮다. Reserve 낮다 for things measured against a level or scale, and use 작다 for the size of a person or object. Note also that 낮다 (low) is a different word from the noun 낮 'daytime' (as in 낮에 = during the day) — same syllable, unrelated meaning. A subtle pairing point: 낮다 vs 짧다 — a low table is 낮은 탁자 (its top sits low), but a short string is 짧은 줄 (little length); 낮다 is vertical position, 짧다 is length. As an adjective it cannot take 있다: 천장이 낮아요, not 낮아 있어요.

mistakes: Saying 그 사람은 키가 낮아요 for 'that person is short' — a person's height uses 작다: 키가 작아요.
Confusing the adjective 낮다 (low) with the noun 낮 (daytime): '낮에 만나요' means 'let's meet during the day,' nothing to do with 낮다.
Forgetting the ㅈ batchim carries over: the 해요-form is 낮아요 (pronounced 'na-ja-yo'), and the past is 낮았어요, not 낮어요.

usage: 얕다 also works figuratively for thin knowledge
adverb 얕게 describes the depth of the action
examples: 이 물은 얕아요.
This water is shallow.
얕다 → 얕아요; the ㅌ batchim links to 얕아요 ('ya-ta-yo')
여기는 바다가 얕아서 아이들이 놀기 좋아요.
The sea is shallow here, so it's good for kids to play.
얕아서 (-아서) connects the shallowness to why it's safe
그 사람은 아는 게 얕아서 깊이 있는 대화가 어려워요.
His knowledge is shallow, so a deep conversation is hard.
real-situation: 얕다 used figuratively for shallow/thin understanding, contrasted with 깊이 (depth)
nuance: 얕다 means SHALLOW — little depth from top to bottom — and its exact opposite is 깊다 (deep). It works both literally (얕은 물 shallow water, 얕은 접시 a shallow dish) and figuratively (얕은 지식 shallow knowledge, 얕은 잠 light sleep). The pitfall for English speakers is hearing 'shallow' and reaching for a color or thinness word: 얕다 is about DEPTH, not about pale color (that's 연하다/옅다) and not about a thin flat object (that's 얇다). Keep three look/sound-alike pairs apart: 얕다 (shallow depth) vs 옅다 (faint/pale, of color or fog) vs 얇다 (thin, of a flat object). Note the spelling — the batchim is ㅌ, so it conjugates 얕아요/얕았어요, and the stem 얕- is unrelated to 얇- despite looking similar. As a descriptive adjective it never takes 있다: 강이 얕아요, not 얕아 있어요.

Mixing 얕다 (shallow depth) with 얇다 (thin, flat): a thin book is 얇은 책, not 얕은 책.
Spelling the batchim wrong — it's 얕다 with ㅌ, conjugating to 얕아요; writing 얄아요 or 얕어요 is incorrect.

usage: to sleep deeply / be a heavy sleeper
the derived noun-and-adverb form of 깊다
examples: 이 강은 깊어요.
This river is deep.
깊다 → 깊어요 (ㅍ batchim, 'gi-peo-yo'); takes 어 because the stem vowel is ㅣ
물이 깊으니까 조심하세요.
The water is deep, so please be careful.
깊으니까 (-으니까) gives a reason that leads to a warning
오랜만에 친구랑 깊은 이야기를 나눴어요.
I had a deep talk with a friend after a long time.
real-situation: 깊은 이야기 = a heart-to-heart; 깊다 carries emotional, not just physical, depth
nuance: 깊다 means DEEP — far from top to bottom (깊은 물 deep water, 깊은 구덩이 a deep hole) — and its opposite is 얕다 (shallow). Beyond the physical, it stretches naturally to deep sleep (잠이 깊다), deep thought (깊은 생각), and close relationships and feelings (정이 깊다), which English also calls 'deep,' so this metaphor transfers well. The English-speaker pitfall is using 깊다 for HEIGHT: a tall building or person is NOT 깊다 — height upward is 높다 (high) or 키가 크다 (tall of a person). 깊다 measures downward/inward depth, 높다 measures upward height; don't let English 'deep voice' mislead you either — a low/deep voice is 목소리가 낮다 (low pitch), not 깊다. Watch the spelling: the batchim is ㅍ, giving 깊어요/깊었어요 (never 깁어요), and the very common derived form 깊이 serves as both the noun 'depth' and the adverb 'deeply.' As an adjective it does not take 있다: 강이 깊어요, not 깊어 있어요.

Saying 목소리가 깊어요 for 'a deep voice' — low vocal pitch is 목소리가 낮아요; 깊다 is for depth, not pitch.
Spelling slip: the 해요-form is 깊어요 (ㅍ batchim), not 깁어요; the past is 깊었어요.

english: to be thick (in diameter); to be coarse
usage: 굵다 = wide in diameter, for long round things
to have a deep, full voice
a thick, resonant voice (a man's low boom)
adverb 굵게; common in cooking instructions
examples: 이 면은 굵어요.
These noodles are thick.
굵다 → 굵어요; the ㄺ batchim reads 'gulg-eo-yo'
채소를 굵게 썰어서 국에 넣었어요.
I cut the vegetables thick and put them in the soup.
굵게 (adverb) tells you how to cut; common recipe phrasing
오늘은 빗방울이 굵어서 우산이 소용없었어요.
The raindrops were so fat today that an umbrella was useless.
real-situation: 비가/빗방울이 굵다 is the idiomatic way to say the rain came down in big, heavy drops
nuance: 굵다 means THICK in the sense of WIDE DIAMETER — thick noodles, a thick rope, thick fingers, a fat tree trunk, bold writing, and even a deep booming voice. Its opposite is 가늘다 (thin/slender in diameter). The crucial English-speaker pitfall is that English 'thick' covers two different Korean ideas: 굵다 is for the cross-section of a long, round, or solid thing, whereas 두껍다 is for the thickness of a FLAT thing (a thick book, a thick blanket, thick paper). So a thick rope is 굵은 밧줄 but a thick book is 두꺼운 책 — never 굵은 책. A natural extension is 비가 굵다 / 빗방울이 굵다 to describe big, fat raindrops (heavy rain). Pronunciation is a hurdle: the ㄺ cluster surfaces as a hard g before a vowel, so 굵어요 is 'gulg-eo-yo' and 굵게 is 'guk-ge.' As a descriptive adjective it cannot take 있다: 줄이 굵어요, not 굵어 있어요.

mistakes: Using 굵다 for a flat object's thickness — a thick book or blanket is 두껍다 (두꺼운 책), not 굵다.
Calling a deep male voice 큰 목소리 (that means loud) when you mean rich/deep — a deep, full voice is 목소리가 굵다.
Mispronouncing the ㄺ cluster — 굵어요 is 'gulg-eo-yo' (the g is pronounced before the vowel), not 'gu-eo-yo.'

english: to be thin; to be slender (in diameter)
usage: before a noun the ㄹ drops → 가는 (not 가늘은)
to have a thin, faint voice
examples: 이 줄은 가늘어요.
This string is thin.
가늘다 → 가늘어요 in the 해요-form (ㄹ stays before a vowel)
파를 가늘게 썰어서 국수에 올렸어요.
I sliced the green onion thin and put it on the noodles.
가늘게 (adverb) = into slender strips; everyday kitchen Korean
할머니 목소리가 점점 가늘어져서 잘 안 들렸어요.
Grandma's voice grew thinner and thinner, so I could barely hear it.
real-situation: 가늘어지다 (-아지다) shows a gradual change to a fainter, thinner voice
nuance: 가늘다 means SLENDER / THIN IN DIAMETER — thin fingers, a thin thread, a thin wire, a faint reedy voice — and its opposite is 굵다 (thick in diameter). The mirror-image pitfall of 굵다 applies: English 'thin' splits into two Korean words. Use 가늘다 for the cross-section of a long or round thing, but use 얇다 for a FLAT thin thing (thin paper, a thin slice of bread, a thin book). So a thin string is 가는 줄 but thin paper is 얇은 종이 — never 가는 종이. Note too that thinness of a PERSON (slim body) is usually 날씬하다 or 말랐다, not 가늘다, which targets a part like fingers or a wrist (손목이 가늘다). The grammar trap: 가늘다 is a ㄹ-stem, so the ㄹ drops before ㄴ — the noun-modifying form is 가는 N (가는 실), not 가늘은 N. In the 해요-form the ㄹ stays: 가늘어요. As an adjective it never takes 있다.

Describing a slim person with 가늘다 — for a slender body say 날씬하다; 가늘다 fits a thin part like 손가락이 가늘다.

english: to be light (in color); to be tender/weak (in strength)
usage: weak/diluted in strength, opposite of 진하다
examples: 색이 연해요.
The color is light (pale).
연하다 → 연해요 (하다-adjective); describes a pale shade
저는 커피를 연하게 마셔요.
I drink my coffee weak.
연하게 (adverb) modifies how you drink it; cafe-ready phrase
이 집 갈비는 고기가 연해서 어른들이 좋아하세요.
The galbi here is so tender that the older folks love it.
real-situation: 연하다 = tender, the praise word for soft meat, with 연해서 (-아서) giving the reason
nuance: 연하다 comes from the hanja 軟 'soft/pliant' and fans out into three everyday senses: light/pale in COLOR (연한 색 a pale color), weak/diluted in STRENGTH (연한 커피 weak coffee, 연한 차 weak tea), and tender in TEXTURE (연한 고기 tender meat). Across color and strength its opposite is 진하다 (dark/deep/strong: 진한 커피 strong coffee, 진한 색 a deep color). The main English-speaker pitfall is using 연하다 for a WEAK PERSON: a frail or physically weak person/body is 약하다 (몸이 약하다), not 연하다 — 연하다 weakens drinks and softens meat, but it does not describe a person's constitution. A second trap is confusing it with 얇다 (physically thin) and 옅다 (faint): pale coffee is 연한/옅은, but a thin sheet is 얇은; keep 'weak/pale/tender' (연하다) apart from 'thin/flat' (얇다). It is a polite, neutral word and shines in cafes and restaurants: '연하게 해 주세요' = please make it weak.

english: to be clear; to be clean/sunny
usage: 맑다 also describes a clear, alert mind
examples: 오늘 하늘이 맑아요.
The sky is clear today.
맑다 → 맑아요; ㄺ reads 'malg-a-yo'; the staple weather sentence
계곡 물이 맑아서 바닥이 다 보여요.
The valley water is so clear you can see all the way to the bottom.
맑아서 (-아서) connects the clearness to the visible result
산에 오니까 공기가 맑아서 기분이 좋아요.
Now that I've come to the mountains, the air is fresh and I feel great.
real-situation: 공기가 맑다 = fresh clean air, paired with -으니까 (now that)
nuance: 맑다 means CLEAR or CLEAN in the sense of pure and transparent — clear see-through water (맑은 물), a cloudless sky (맑은 하늘 = sunny), fresh unpolluted air (맑은 공기), a clear ringing sound or a clear alert mind (정신이 맑다). Its opposite is 흐리다 (cloudy/murky). The key English-speaker pitfall is using 맑다 for a tidy ROOM: English 'clean' covers both purity and tidiness, but a clean, tidy room is 깨끗하다 (방이 깨끗하다), not 맑다. Reserve 맑다 for natural clearness/transparency (water, sky, air, sound) and use 깨끗하다 for cleanliness/neatness of objects and spaces. As a weather word it pairs with 날씨 and 하늘 and is the standard term in forecasts: 내일은 맑겠습니다 (it will be clear/sunny tomorrow). Pronunciation: the ㄺ surfaces as g before a vowel, so 맑아요 is 'malg-a-yo' and 맑게 is 'mak-ge.' As a descriptive adjective it never takes 있다: 물이 맑아요, not 맑아 있어요.

english: to be cloudy; to be blurry/murky
usage: 흐리다 also fits a faint, fuzzy memory
examples: 오늘 날씨가 흐려요.
The weather is cloudy today.
흐리다 → 흐려요 (ㅣ + 어 contracts to 려); core weather word
비가 와서 강물이 흐려졌어요.
It rained, so the river water turned murky.
흐려지다 (-아지다) = became murky; shows the change of state
사진이 흐려서 글씨가 잘 안 보여요.
The photo is blurry, so I can't read the text well.
real-situation: 흐리다 = blurry/out of focus, with 흐려서 (-아서) giving the reason
nuance: 흐리다 is the all-purpose word for 'unclear,' covering CLOUDY weather (흐린 날 an overcast day), MURKY water (흐린 물), and BLURRY/out-of-focus images or hazy memories (사진이 흐리다, 기억이 흐리다). Its opposite is 맑다 (clear), and for weather these two are the everyday pair: 맑아요 (clear/sunny) ↔ 흐려요 (cloudy). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 흐리다 to mean DIRTY: murky water that's hard to see through is 흐리다, but water or a surface that is dirty/filthy is 더럽다 — 흐리다 is about lack of CLARITY, not presence of grime. Note also a near-synonym for blurriness: 뿌옇다/희미하다 also describe a hazy, faint look, but 흐리다 is the plain default learners should master first. The conjugation trap: like other ㅣ-stems, 흐리다 contracts in the 해요-form to 흐려요 (not 흐리어요), past 흐렸어요. As a descriptive adjective it does not take 있다: 하늘이 흐려요, not 흐려 있어요.

english: to be hard; to be firm/solid
usage: 단단하다 = firm and solid to the touch
adverb 단단하게 for a secure knot
단단하다 extends to a firm, resolute mind
examples: 이 빵이 단단해요.
This bread is hard.
단단하다 → 단단해요 (하다-adjective); describes firm texture
끈을 단단하게 묶어서 안 풀려요.
I tied the string firmly, so it won't come undone.
단단하게 (adverb) = securely; ties the firmness to the result
덜 익어서 감자가 아직 단단해요.
The potatoes are still firm because they're undercooked.
real-situation: 단단하다 for food that hasn't softened yet, with 덜 (not fully) + reason
nuance: 단단하다 means HARD, FIRM, or SOLID to the touch — a hard rock, solid ice, firm undercooked potatoes, a tightly-tied knot, well-packed ground — and it extends warmly to a person who is steady, tough-minded, and dependable (마음이 단단하다 mentally strong). Its opposite is 부드럽다 (soft) or 무르다 (mushy/yielding). The nuance English speakers miss is the difference from 딱딱하다: both translate as 'hard,' but 단단하다 has a positive ring of solid, sturdy, well-put-together firmness, while 딱딱하다 stresses STIFF, RIGID, unpleasant hardness — stale rock-hard bread is 딱딱한 빵, and a stiff, awkward atmosphere is 분위기가 딱딱하다 (you would never say 단단한 분위기). So choose 단단하다 when 'firm/solid/sturdy' is a good thing, and 딱딱하다 when 'stiff/rigid' is the point. It is a regular 하다-adjective: 단단해요 / 단단했어요, and as an adjective it does not take 있다.

Using 단단하다 for a hard/difficult task — 'hard' as in difficult is 어렵다, not 단단하다; 단단하다 is only physical/mental firmness.
Limiting 단단하다 to food only — it also fits firm ground (땅이 단단하다), a tight knot, and a steady mind (마음이 단단하다).

usage: before a noun the ㄹ drops → 둥근 (not 둥글은)
둥글다 for the overall round form of an object
to have an easygoing, agreeable nature
둥글다 also means smooth/non-prickly in personality
adverb 둥글게 = in a round arrangement
examples: 공은 둥글어요.
A ball is round.
둥글다 → 둥글어요 in the 해요-form (ㄹ stays before a vowel)
보름달이 둥글게 떴어요.
The full moon came up round.
둥글게 (adverb) describes the round shape it shows; 보름달 = full moon
사람들이 둥글게 둘러앉아서 이야기를 나눴어요.
People sat around in a circle and talked.
real-situation: 둥글게 둘러앉다 = to sit gathered in a ring; a natural set phrase
nuance: 둥글다 means ROUND — having a rounded, circular, or spherical form: a round moon, a round table, a ball, a round face. Beyond shape it has a lovely figurative use for personality: 성격이 둥글다 means easygoing, agreeable, and non-confrontational (literally 'rounded,' i.e. no sharp edges). The fine line learners blur is 둥글다 vs 동그랗다: both mean 'round,' but 둥글다 is the broader, often three-dimensional 'rounded' (a globe, a face, a mound), while 동그랗다 feels SMALL, NEAT, and precisely circular (a little dot, round wide eyes: 눈이 동그래지다 = eyes go round with surprise). The grammar trap is the ㄹ-stem rule: the ㄹ drops before ㄴ, so the noun-modifying form is 둥근 N (둥근 얼굴, 둥근 달), never 둥글은. In the 해요-form the ㄹ stays: 둥글어요. The related noun is 동그라미 (a drawn circle). As an adjective it does not take 있다.

english: to be pointy; to be sharp (in shape)
usage: a clever way out / a good solution
idiom: 뾰족한 수가 없다 = no good solution
examples: 연필이 뾰족해요.
The pencil is sharp (pointy).
뾰족하다 → 뾰족해요 (하다-adjective); about the pointed tip
이 가위는 끝이 뾰족해서 조심해야 해요.
The tip of these scissors is pointy, so you have to be careful.
끝이 뾰족하다 = the end is pointed; 뾰족해서 (-아서) gives the reason for caution
좋은 방법을 찾아봤지만 뾰족한 수가 없네요.
I looked for a good way, but there's no clever solution.
real-situation: idiomatic 뾰족한 수가 없다 = no bright/sure-fire way out
nuance: 뾰족하다 describes a POINTY, sharp-TIPPED SHAPE — a sharpened pencil, a pointed roof, a peaked mountain, the pointy end of scissors. The key distinction from 날카롭다 is shape vs cutting power: 뾰족하다 is about coming to a POINT, whereas 날카롭다 is about a keen, SHARP EDGE that cuts (a knife) — and 날카롭다 also extends to a sharp/cutting tone or gaze (날카로운 눈빛), which 뾰족하다 does not. So a well-sharpened knife is 칼이 날카롭다 (cuts well), while the tip being pointed is 칼끝이 뾰족하다 (shape). There is a very common idiom to memorize: 뾰족한 수가 없다 = 'there's no clever/sure solution,' a set phrase you'll hear when someone is stuck. Spelling is the trap: it is 뾰 with the double consonant ㅃ plus ㅛ — write 뾰족하다, not 뽀족하다 or 뾰쪽하다. It's a regular 하다-adjective: 뾰족해요 / 뾰족했어요, and as an adjective it does not take 있다.

Applying 뾰족하다 to a sharp tone or sharp eyes — a cutting gaze/voice is 날카롭다 (날카로운 눈빛), not 뾰족한 눈빛.

english: to be flat; to be even/level
usage: 평평하다 = an even surface, no bumps or slope
smooth, level path with no inclines
to spread out flat / smooth out
a level base, good for placing things
examples: 이 길은 평평해요.
This road is flat.
평평하다 → 평평해요 (하다-adjective); about a smooth, level surface
바닥이 평평해서 책상을 놓기 좋아요.
The floor is level, so it's good for setting up a desk.
평평해서 (-아서) links the levelness to why it's convenient
텐트를 치려고 평평한 곳을 찾았어요.
I looked for a flat spot to pitch the tent.
real-situation: 평평한 곳 = a level patch of ground, exactly what you need for camping
nuance: 평평하다 means FLAT and LEVEL — an even surface with no bumps, dips, or slopes: level ground, a flat road, a smooth level floor or tabletop. It is built from the repeated Sino-Korean syllable 平 'flat/level' (平平), the very same 平 in 평지 (flatland) and 평야 (a plain), so the root literally doubles down on 'level.' Two confusions to avoid. First, the look-alike 평범하다 (平凡 'ordinary/common'): it sounds and looks similar but means 'ordinary, average, nothing special' about a person or thing — never use 평평하다 for that. Second, 납작하다: that describes something SQUASHED FLAT or low-profile (a flat squashed box, a flat nose), i.e. flattened in thickness, whereas 평평하다 describes a surface being EVEN and level. So flat level ground is 평평한 땅, but a flattened/squashed shape is 납작한 상자. It is a regular 하다-adjective: 평평해요 / 평평했어요, and as an adjective it does not take 있다.
